papers.abstract: Real-time decoding of the surface code is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and scaling the decoder to large code distances in hardware remains a challenge. The locality of Union-Find (UF) decoding makes it a leading candidate for such a decoder in distributed hardware. Prior distributed UF decoders, however, map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto an array of processing elements (PEs) under a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, and a three-dimensional array of PEs scales poorly on planar hardware. This paper presents Amatlas, a two-dimensional PE array for UF decoding that operates without a central controller. Amatlas assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the two-dimensional qubit lattice and stores the states of all measurement rounds in the local memory of the PE, so every link connects adjacent PEs in the array. Every PE advances on every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization, and the clock is the only global signal of the array. Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation of Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, where the average decoding time is 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%. Amatlas achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared with 0.78% reported for UF decoding under the same noise model.
authors: Takuya Kasamura, Leo Itoh, Seita Tsuboi, Hidetsugu Irie, Junichiro Kadomoto

papers.title: Dimensional crossover to a slow disordered spin bath below the mean spin spacing
papers.abstract: How thin must a layer of spins be to act as a two-dimensional bath? For nitrogen spins around an NV$^-$ centre in diamond, a cluster expansion with flip-flopping outer spins gives a crossover near the mean spin spacing. Thin layers follow two-dimensional scaling with a prefactor six to seven times that of bulk. Without hyperfine disorder the crossover remains but the step is under three: the disorder leaves each spin almost no resonant partner. Flip-flops allow several milliseconds, so another process must set the measured 0.5 ms; nitrogen spin-lattice relaxation is consistent.

papers.title: On-Demand Tailoring of High-Dimensional Orbital Angular Momentum States via a Phase-Only Hologram
papers.abstract: Photonic orbital angular momentum (OAM) provides a naturally discrete and unbounded Hilbert space for high-dimensional encoding and has emerged as a powerful degree of freedom for advanced information processing. On-demand tailoring of both the amplitude and phase profiles of high-dimensional OAM states is essential for numerous applications, particularly in quantum information science. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate an efficient method for achieving such on-demand tailoring using a purely phase-only modulation scheme. The measured fidelity remains above 80% even for a 128-dimensional state, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Compared with previous techniques, our method achieves significantly higher generation efficiency, and this advantage becomes more pronounced as the dimensionality increases. Moreover, our approach substantially reduces experimental complexity while maintaining precise control, thereby offering a practical and scalable solution for high-dimensional OAM state engineering in both classical and quantum information processing.
authors: Hao Sheng, Zi-Shuo Wang, Sheng-Qiang Jia, Zi-Mo Cheng, Li Fan, Jianping Ding, Jia-Min Xu, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang

papers.title: Superconductivity from the Berry connection from many-electron wave functions: $U(1)$ gauge fluctuation, gauge invariance, and superconductivity
papers.abstract: The electromagnetic $U(1)$ gauge invariance and superconductivity are examined by employing the Berry connection from many-electron wave functions and the fluctuations of it that give rise to the probabilistic random transitions among quantum states. The gauge invariance in the classical electrodynamics is regarded as the requirement that extracts unaffected parts by the gauge fluctuation. In quantum mechanics, dissipation-free states from the gauge fluctuation exist, and we identify them as superconducting states. We explain the reversible superconducting-normal phase transition in a magnetic field including the force balance. The present superconductivity theory lifts two fundamental disagreements between theory and experiment existing in the current standard theory with keeping the major results by the BCS theory. Thus, it may be considered as a superconductivity theory encompassing the current standard one.

papers.title: When Malus' Law Meets the Wigner-Bell Inequality: Violation by Nonseparable Classical Light
papers.abstract: Bell-type inequalities are commonly associated with quantum nonlocality, yet their mathematical structure also reflects more general constraints on the joint probability distributions assigned to measurements performed in different contexts. Here we examine this distinction through the Wigner--Bell inequality using a classical optical field with two nonseparable degrees of freedom. Starting from a subsystem response-factorization assumption, we derive a Wigner-type probability bound requiring the pairwise measurement statistics to be compatible with a single nonnegative global joint distribution. For a classically nonseparable optical field, the corresponding joint probabilities are represented directly by normalized joint intensities and obey Malus' law. We show that these Malus-law probabilities violate the Wigner--Bell bound over a finite range of analyzer settings. The violation does not imply spatial nonlocality or a failure of classical electrodynamics. Rather, it demonstrates the incompatibility of context-dependent optical projection statistics with the global probability assignment underlying the Wigner construction. We further derive an extended Wigner-Bell bound for general imperfect correlations and propose an interferometric experiment for reconstructing the required joint probabilities from intensity measurements. These results provide a transparent optical realization of the probabilistic structure behind Bell-type inequalities and help distinguish consequences of Hilbert-space structure, nonseparability, and measurement context from those specifically associated with quantum nonlocality.

papers.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More
papers.abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on $n$ cities in $O^*(2^n)$ time. To date, no $\Oh(c^n)$-time classical algorithm is known for any $c<2$. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time $O^*(1.7274^n)$, which is still the best known quantum time bound. In this work, we improve the running time to $O^*(1.70961^n)$. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.

papers.title: Exclusion and internal structure in the association/dissociation kinetics of DNA-binding proteins in the fast diffusion limit
papers.abstract: In many canonical biophysical and biochemical contexts, complex diffusing DNA-binding proteins undergoing nonspecific adsorption and desorption can exist in different conformational states. Equilibrium binding theories and kinetic models of competing ligands provide a basis for describing these systems. Coupling the internal conformational kinetics of bound proteins to exclusion and diffusion requires tracking both protein positions and binding states. Closed-form, tractable mathematical models that accurately describe the stochastic dynamics of structured proteins that bind to and diffuse along DNA are lacking. Here, we develop a new coarse-grained stochastic model of nonspecific DNA-protein binding in the fast diffusion regime, from which we derive an effective Markov model and its corresponding mean-field approximation that incorporates protein footprint size and conformational switching. We fit our new model quantitatively to previously measured dynamics of Replication Protein A (RPA) binding to ssDNA. Finally, by including multisegment binding states, our analysis captures facilitated exchange, revealing how multisegment architecture balances high affinity with rapid remodeling. Our theoretical model applies broadly to many other DNA-binding protein systems, including nucleosomes, ssDNA-binding proteins, and other multisegment complexes, providing accurate predictions and new strategies for evaluating experimental data.

papers.title: Late-time OTOCs in Toda conformal field theory
papers.abstract: We study late-time out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) of semi-degenerate primary fields in two-dimensional $A_{N-1}$ Toda conformal field theory. In Liouville theory ($N=2$), we find that the OTOC decays as $t^{-3/2}$ when the continuum edge dominates, correcting a previously reported constant limit. For $N=3$, a transverse contour pinch reduces the spectral integral to one dimension. Assuming that the reduced expansion is complete, in the continuous phase the regulated edge behaves as a discrete state, and the OTOC approaches a pure braiding phase. As we check numerically, the edge block is a free-field correlator in a charge-neutral Weyl frame; this explains the pure phase and is consistent with crossing symmetry. For both $N=2$ and $N=3$, a dominant discrete residue gives a constant late-time limit. For $N\geq4$, the same one-dimensional reduction violates a crossing bound on the lowest intermediate weight of a positive diagonal expansion. Hence the $N=2,3$ phase diagram does not extend to higher rank without additional contributions below the reduced continuum edge or outside a positive diagonal expansion.

papers.title: A Nonlocal Allen--Cahn Model for Volume-Constrained Wetting and Its Multi-Structure-Preserving Discretization
papers.abstract: At finite interface thickness, small droplets can shrink or disappear during wetting relaxation even when the phase-field mass is conserved. We develop a nonlocal Allen--Cahn model that couples a nonlinear diffuse-volume constraint to dynamic wall relaxation through Onsager's principle. The constraint gradient vanishes at the pure-phase values and does zero work in the energy balance, preserving the original bulk and wall dissipation structure. We construct a Compatible Variational Chain-Rule (CVC) scheme using the same discrete derivative of the volume density in the correction and in the volume increment. The scheme exactly conserves the nonlinear diffuse volume and reproduces the bulk--wall dissipation identity for the original discrete energy. Under a coercivity condition, the energy also yields a mesh-dependent maximum-norm bound. Numerical tests show second-order convergence in space and time. In flat-wall tests, the proposed model improves small-droplet retention and geometric-volume preservation and reproduces equilibrium cap shapes and contact angles. Additional tests illustrate wetting on chemically heterogeneous and rough substrates.
authors: Yadong Liu, Nan Lu, Zhonghua Qiao, Yuze Zhang

papers.title: Structure theorem for quantum limit cycle attractors: A geometric path-integral approach
papers.abstract: We show a Structure Theorem for an arbitrary separable quantum system (\(\dim\mathcal{H}\leq\aleph_0\)) that is coupled, through a symmetric bidirectional phase interface, to a self-sustaining phase-oscillator environment. Under the assumptions of \(U(1)\) covariance, instantaneous Lindblad bounded positivity, and the existence of an entrainable periodic attractor, the reduced generator is forced into a universal operator structure consisting of a state-dependent coherent recoil together with single-quantum feedback. Positivity further imposes a sharp dimensional dichotomy: purely dissipative gain saturation is forbidden in finite dimensions by trace-norm contraction, so coherent feedback is mandatory for qubits and qudits, whereas unbounded ladder algebras permit purely dissipative saturation. Expanding the general feedback functionals to leading order in the coupling recovers a canonical polynomial master equation that remains completely positive and trace-preserving in every dimension and combines additively with ordinary linear Lindblad channels. An accompanying Inverse Coupling Theorem shows that an autonomous periodic orbit can be sustained only when the interaction manifold has non-trivial fundamental group \(\pi_1(\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{Z}\), thereby isolating the sinusoidal \(U(1)\)-covariant phase coupling as the generic mechanism. The resulting implementation is realized explicitly for a single qubit, a bipartite two-qubit system, and a bosonic Fock space.

papers.title: Existence of single-resonance parametric bound states in the continuum: System of Schr\"odinger equations
papers.abstract: A bound state in the continuum (BIC) is an eigenmode of a linear wave system with its eigen-frequency embedded in the radiation continuum of scattering states. At the frequency of a BIC, scattering problems with given incident waves from infinity lose uniqueness. Due to their close connection with strong resonance effects, BICs have found many useful applications in classical and quantum wave systems. Existence theories of BICs have been established for some cases involving the so-called symmetry-protected BICs, Friedrich-Wintgen BICs, and Fabry-Perot BICs. The single-resonance parametric BICs (srp-BICs) are another important class of BICs. Such a BIC emerges from a single resonant state through tuning a real parameter. Using a simple system of two one-dimensional Schr\"odinger equations, we demonstrate the formation of srp-BICs and establish a rigorous existence theory.

papers.title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.

papers.title: Controlling truncation errors in loop tensor network renormalization
papers.abstract: At finite bond dimension $\chi$, tensor network renormalization (TNR) of a critical model eventually becomes gapped. For LoopTNR with $O(2)$ symmetry on the $c=1$ critical line of the six-vertex model, parametrized by the Luttinger parameter $K$, we show that the correlation length $\xi$ of the gapped phase is set by the seed of the dimerization injected by the truncation, and depends on $\chi$ only through it. Read from a weak-coupling window early in the same run, the seed predicts $\xi=10^3$-$10^{16}$ via the sine-Gordon mass-coupling relation with no free parameter, to within a few percent for $K\le1.5$ and about 10% at $K=1.75$; since the seed fluctuates strongly with $\chi$, $\xi$ is not monotonic in $\chi$. An alternation of the vertex weights shifts the seed; with its sign read from a $\pi$ twist, one short calibration predicts a counterterm that delays the breakdown in 16 of the 17 compensated groups of a campaign fixed in advance. A correction of the coarse-grained tensors, repeated during the flow, keeps the runs at $K=1$ and $1.5$ critical up to step 160, the last step computed, and exposes the marginal truncation error that remains. Our findings illustrate a systematic procedure for controlling the relevant truncation error, and thereby extending the critical window, in tensor network renormalization at finite bond dimension.
authors: Rikuto Fushio, Kokin Cho, Yuta Yamamoto, Akira Otsuki, Masahito Yamazaki

papers.title: On a new resolution of the identity for coherent states of the Euclidean group E(2)
papers.abstract: We provide a non-divergent resolution of the identity for coherent states of the Euclidean group $E(2)$, replacing the integral on the whole group with the Haar measure by an invariant integration with non local kernels constructed by Steinberg and Wolf in 1981, valid for solutions of Helmholtz equation, that appears in natural way as the eigenvalue equation of the Casimir operator of $E(2)$. With this construction, all properties of Perelomov coherent states are preserved, in particular covariance, and all square-integrable functions are addmissible, improving previous results like those of de Bi\`evre and Torr\'esani.

papers.title: A bright source of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs based on beam-like Type-II SPDC
papers.abstract: Bright sources of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs are increasingly required for the rapid advancement of quantum technologies. However, simultaneously achieving high brightness and high-dimensional spatial entanglement through spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a bright source of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs using beam-like Type-II SPDC in a $\beta$-barium borate crystal. Compared with a conventional collinear Type-I source, it exhibits a $\sim$1.56-fold enhancement in the detected single-photon count rate and a $\sim$1.45-fold enhancement in the coincidence count rate. Measurements of position correlations and momentum anti-correlations certify at least 62-dimensional spatial entanglement within a 121-dimensional basis. These correlations are further exploited to demonstrate quantum imaging in both the position and momentum domains. These characteristics make the source a practical resource for high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies.
authors: Ming Zhang, Zhiming Qing, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Jianping Ding, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang

papers.title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm for the Generalised Geography Game
papers.abstract: The Generalized Geography Game ($GGG$) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a directed graph, where players alternately move a token along edges without revisiting previously visited vertices. In the existing literature, determining whether an arbitrary position in a graph is a winning position for either player is a well-known $PSPACE$-complete decision problem. Certain formulations of $GGG$ have been shown to fall outside the $PSPACE$-complete complexity class. While $PSPACE$-complete problems are believed to take exponential time for classical computation, quantum computation offers new possibilities. In this work, we present a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time ($BQP$) algorithm for solving the $GGG$ problem. The proposed algorithm runs in time $O(N^{2}/\epsilon^{6})$, which is polynomial in the input size $N$, and achieves bounded error with $\epsilon = O(1/\mathrm{poly}(N))$. This result demonstrates the potential of quantum algorithms to efficiently solve combinatorial game problems that are traditionally considered computationally hard in the classical setting.

papers.title: Reproducible distributions of energy-relaxation times in superconducting qubits from broadband SWAP spectroscopy
papers.abstract: The distribution of the qubit energy-relaxation time (T1) in a superconducting quantum processor affects its logical error rates. However, reports on qubit fabrication quality focus on the median or best-case T1 from measurements that are not reproducible due to resonant coupling to two-level system (TLS) defects whose frequencies fluctuate in time. Here, we sweep the frequency f01 of a flux-tunable qubit over several GHz with SWAP spectroscopy, quoting the quality factor Q = 2 pi f01 T1 to make T1 comparable across frequencies. We show that the cumulative distribution of Q pooled over the sweep is reproducible across four thermal cycles spanning 326 days, up to the reshuffling of strongly coupled TLSs. In contrast to repeated measurements at a single frequency, the medians of the broadband Q distributions spread by an order of magnitude less over 3 days. The distance between the cumulative distributions of repeats comes close to its sampling floor only for the broadband sweeps. The broadband Q distribution further resolves small coherence differences between identically designed qubits on two dies of the same wafer. These results establish the broadband Q distribution as a reproducible metric for qubit fabrication quality.
authors: Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Maximilien F. Debbas, Ana Vald\'es-Curiel, Ming-Han Chou, Haifeng Qiao, Shahriar Aghaeimeibodi, Oskar Painter, Matthew H. Matheny, Loren J. Swenson

papers.title: How Many Autonomous Encoded Qubits Force an Isotropic Noise Response?
papers.abstract: Depolarizing noise scales trace distances by a common factor. An encoded qubit is autonomous if its reduced input state determines its output. For $D=2^n\ge4$, autonomy forces this isotropy at a sharp threshold of $(D^2+5)/3$ generic encodings, two more than state tomography requires. For Pauli noise, one generic encoding suffices. With one-bit readouts and no quantum memory or reference, switching encodings cuts the worst-case cost for the Pauli test by a factor of $D$, up to logarithms. For any family, a channel with leakage $O(D^{-3/2})$ can transmit one bit perfectly and erase another.

papers.title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
papers.abstract: Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation. We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.
authors: Xiaoran Li, Zhi Yin, Zhupeng Han, Zhengquan Pan, Kangyu Zheng

papers.title: Decoherent Histories from Local Spectral Dephasing in Quantum Many-Body Systems
papers.abstract: We study local spectral dephasing as a mechanism for decoherent histories in isolated quantum many-body systems. We prove that vanishing projector-weighted spectral concentration is asymptotically equivalent to vanishing time-averaged local memory. With independently sampled waiting times and suitable conditions on the initial state and history weights, this local property suppresses normalized interference across complete fixed-length history families with high probability. For translation-invariant lattices, spectral estimates provide conditions under which dephasing occurs at long times. Exact diagonalization and sparse time evolution of a spin chain illustrate the results.

papers.title: Almost sure lower bound for the Hausdorff dimension of the spectrum of critical AMO
papers.abstract: We show that there exists an absolute constant $d>0$ such that for almost all frequencies $\alpha\in[0,1]\setminus\Q$, the Hausdorff dimension of the spectrum of the critical almost Mathieu operator $H_{1,\alpha,\theta}$ is bounded from below by $d$.

papers.title: Phonon-Aware Electron-to-Nuclear Spin Quantum Memory in NV Centers
papers.abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a promising solid-state platform for quantum memory: the electron spin can be optically initialized and read out, while nearby nuclear spins have long coherence times and can serve as storage qubits. In this work, we develop a phonon-aware open quantum system model for electron-to-nuclear spin state transfer in a single NV center. The model includes the NV electron spin, a coupled 13C nuclear spin, the hyperfine interaction, an effective microwave/radio-frequency-assisted SWAP interaction for writing and reading, a single effective phonon mode with longitudinal spin-phonon coupling, and Lindblad relaxation and dephasing channels. The dynamics are simulated with the Lindblad master equation in QuTiP, using the secular approximation and a hyperfine-resonant drive in the rotating frame. Without spin-phonon coupling and electron decoherence, the write-store-read protocol recovers the stored state with a fidelity above 0.9999. With the default decoherence rates, increasing the spin-phonon coupling from 0 to 0.06 MHz lowers the worst-case retrieval fidelity from 0.9994 to 0.9884, and the fidelity oscillates with the phonon-mode period because electron-phonon entanglement generated during the write step is partially undone during the read step. With a phenomenological temperature-dependent rate model, the fidelity decreases monotonically from 0.9997 at 1 K to 0.9938 at 300 K, while storage-time losses follow the assumed nuclear-spin decoherence rates. The storage-time plots, temperature sweep, and parameter maps identify operating regimes for NV-center quantum memory, and the accompanying open-source code provides a reproducible framework for studying phonon-limited quantum memory.

papers.title: Empirical De-Quantization and Norm-Controlled Spectral Audit of Quantum Cognition Machine Learning in an Emerging Equity Market
papers.abstract: Quantum-inspired machine learning in econophysics describes states of financial markets through matrix Hamiltonians, using ground-state expectations to predict returns and spectral gaps to identify crises. Although early work reports encouraging advances, it remains unclear whether these stem from genuine noncommutative quantum geometry or from conventional classical regularization and scale effects. We test this in a controlled audit of matrix-form Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML) and variational quantum circuits on the Moscow Exchange (2020-2025), combining daily equity data with causally lagged macro news under realistic trading costs, short-selling bans, and abrupt shifts in market regimes. By using capacity-matched operator swaps -- which progressively eliminate complex Berry phases and matrix noncommutativity down to a commuting classical Gibbs radial-basis limit under scale-invariant regularization -- as well as testing spectral indicators against radial-norm null hypotheses and untrained GUE random matrices, we isolate the contribution of each quantum element. In out-of-sample data, neither complex phases, noncommutativity, nor circuit entanglement improves the ranking of returns relative to classical controls. Once feature magnitudes are normalized, apparent crisis detection from raw spectral gaps drops below chance levels. These results show that on noisy equity panels, matrix-form QCML acts as an adaptive spectrally bounded classical smoothing kernel: it reliably integrates lagged news and curbs extreme crisis forecasts without passing economic multiple-testing thresholds, while our audit provides operator-swap and random-matrix controls for evaluating future quantum-inspired financial models.

papers.title: Gaussian Is All You Need: Renyi Optimizers and Optical Channel Simulation
papers.abstract: Preparing an entangled state faithfully requires an amount of resource given by its entanglement cost. With less entanglement, the best achievable fidelity is governed by the R\'enyi entanglement of formation of orders above one. We prove that, for any finite-energy multimode bosonic Gaussian state, all these quantities are additive and attained by a Gaussian pure-state decomposition. It follows that the closest separable state in fidelity to any Gaussian state is Gaussian, and that the strong converse exponent of entanglement dilution, which sets how fast the optimal fidelity decays below the cost, is exactly computable. For channels, we prove that pure Gaussian inputs minimize the output R\'enyi entropies of every multimode Gaussian channel at all orders $\alpha\ge1$, and we obtain the optimal fidelity of simulating pure-loss and quantum-limited amplifier channels with finite entanglement, for any number of uses.

papers.title: Gradient-flow scale setting from octet baryon masses in N$^3$LO covariant chiral perturbation theory
papers.abstract: We determine the gradient-flow scale $t_0$ by analyzing the lowest-lying octet-baryon masses on the Coordinated Lattice Simulations (CLS) $N_f=2+1$ ensembles in covariant baryon chiral perturbation theory up to next-to-next-to-next-to leading order (N$^3$LO). By including the finite-volume corrections self-consistently and the discretization effects from Symanzik effective field theory, we obtain a good description of the RQCD data and determine the gradient-flow scale to be $\sqrt{8t_{0,\mathrm{ph}}}=0.4120(14)_\mathrm{stat.}(16)_\mathrm{sys.}$ fm with sub-percent precision. The predicted octet baryon masses agree well with the experimental values in the isospin limit. Using the Feynman-Hellmann theorem, we also estimate the nucleon sigma terms, which are consistent with direct determinations from three-point correlation functions on the same CLS ensembles.

papers.title: Coherent quantum-circuit simulation of Mueller dipole branching at small $x$: multiplicity fluctuations and DIS phenomenology
papers.abstract: Mueller dipole branching at small $x$ is a stochastic process in which splitting rates depend on transverse geometry. We construct a coherent quantum circuit for a regulated finite-state version of this process. Poisson-clock uniformization controls the number of updates, while orthogonal event-history registers retain the splitting paths, including those leading to the same final configuration. The circuit prepares transition amplitudes from local splitting rates rather than loading a precomputed evolved distribution. Its statevector multiplicity probabilities reproduce the truncated-clock Markov result to numerical precision and agree with the full continuous-time Markov-chain benchmark within approximately $7\times10^{-4}$. To examine fluctuations beyond the small circuit, we independently simulate the Mueller cascade with continuous transverse coordinates. At the largest rapidity studied, its normalized fourth factorial moment is $1.81$, compared with $2.84$ for an equal-mean Yule process. We also determine multiplicity entropies and correlations between dipole-size sectors. Applying a fixed negative-binomial dipole-to-charged-particle response reproduces the rising trend of the H1 charged-particle multiplicity entropy toward smaller $x$, but does not fully describe the measured multiplicity distributions. These results demonstrate an explicit coherent encoding of finite-state dipole branching and clarify its relation to continuous-cascade fluctuations and DIS phenomenology.

papers.title: Universal Work Extraction from Individual Sequences by Finite--State Information Engines
papers.abstract: We consider information engines that interact with a heat bath at temperature $T$, a work reservoir, and a tape carrying an individual (deterministic) sequence $x$ over a finite alphabet $\X$. An engine is a cascade of autonomous ratchets with fixed energy levels and detailed--balance dynamics, each processing segments of $m$ tape cells and having finitely many internal states. We prove a converse bound on the extractable work in terms of the empirical block entropies of $x$,and show that it is achievable \emph{universally}, by engines whose energy levels do not depend on $x$. The maximal work per symbol is $kT[\ln|\X|-\bar H(x)]$, where $k$ is Boltzmann's constant and $\bar H(x)$ is the asymptotic normalized aligned block entropy of $x$, which equals its block Lempel--Ziv complexity, and the minimal work needed to erase $x$ is $kT\bar H(x)$ per symbol. Underlying these results is a two--way correspondence with universal coding: energy levels define a code, and a suitably operated cascade extracts $kT$ times $\ln|\X|$ per symbol minus the code length; conversely, a fluctuation identity shows that every engine fixed in advance defines a code. Hence, converses of universal coding apply verbatim to engines; e.g., the optimal redundancy of memoryless universal engines is given by the Shtarkov sum.

papers.title: Unified preparation of exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scars from Dicke states
papers.abstract: We propose a unified quantum algorithm for preparing exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scar (QMBS) states in the spin-1 {\it XY}, domain-wall-conserving, and Onsager scar models. Model-dependent isometries map the exact scar states to Dicke states and the target asymptotic QMBS states to gapless magnon excitations of the spin-1/2 ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain. Exact QMBS states are prepared by applying the inverse isometries to Dicke states. For asymptotic QMBS states, block encoding first prepares the magnon excitations from Dicke states to a prescribed fidelity, after which the inverse isometries map the prepared states back to the physical chains. At fixed target fidelity, the block-encoding success probability has a positive lower bound independent of system size and scar index, implying that a constant number of amplitude amplification rounds suffices. Our algorithm enables systematic studies of nonergodic dynamics on programmable quantum simulators.
authors: Yuki Asari, Masaya Kunimi, Tetsuro Nikuni

papers.title: Exploring Physical Mechanisms Underlying the Emergence of Collective Order
papers.abstract: Emergence of collective order from disordered constituents is a hallmark of active matter, and the Vicsek model (VM) serves as a paradigmatic system for its study. However, whether density-induced emergence in the VM differs between angular (intrinsic) and vectorial (extrinsic) noise, and what mechanisms govern the transitions, remain largely unexplored. Remarkably, we uncover that collective order emerges from a disordered state in a continuous-like manner under intrinsic noise but abruptly under extrinsic noise. Combining nonequilibrium landscape-flux theory with a coarse-grained mapping method, we show that the landscape evolves continuously from a single basin to two and back to one under intrinsic noise, but the two-basin landscape appears abruptly under extrinsic noise across the critical transition to flocking. The counterclockwise nonequilibrium flux sustains global circular motion, providing the driving force for reshaping the landscape. The mean flux and entropy production rate change steeply near the emergence threshold and exhibit pronounced peaks within the coexistence region, identifying them as the dynamical and thermodynamic origins of emergence. Our findings reveal a distinct abrupt emergence under extrinsic noise and offer deeper mechanistic insight, practical applications (e.g., locating phase boundaries and distinguishing transition types), and extensibility to other nonequilibrium collective systems.
authors: Yitong Cai, Ruizhe Yan, Dongrun Jian, Jie Su, Jin Wang

papers.title: Rotation curves of dwarf galaxies and dark matter as a condensate of $q$-deformed bosons: reconstruction and fits of the deformation profile
papers.abstract: Dark-matter-dominated dwarf galaxies are a sensitive testing ground for models in which dark matter is a self-interacting Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). In the Thomas-Fermi limit the standard BEC halo has the density profile $\rho\propto\sin(kr)/(kr)$, so that the shape of its rotation curve is fixed up to two scale parameters. Here we consider a condensate of $q$-deformed bosons. We show that, in the Thomas-Fermi limit, the deformation enters the structure of the halo only through the chemical potential of the condensate; consequently, a spatially uniform deformation parameter leaves the standard BEC profile unchanged. In every galaxy $\chi$ is depressed in the inner region, $kr\lesssim1$, relative to the outer halo, where it is approximately constant in most cases: the standard condensate describes the outer halo, while the core requires a weaker deformation, i.e., $q$ closer to unity. The profiles share this qualitative shape, but neither the depth nor the width of the depression is universal. Modelling the depression by a Gaussian, with two additional parameters, we fit the rotation curves with rms residuals of $0.6$--$2.6$~km\,s$^{-1}$, against $1.6$--$8.5$~km\,s$^{-1}$ for the standard condensate. According to the Bayesian information criterion, the deformed condensate is preferred over the standard condensate, the Navarro-Frenk-White profile, and the Burkert profile in four galaxies, is indistinguishable from the best of them in two, and is disfavoured in two. We discuss the limitations of these results, in particular the absence of error bars in the data, the neglect of baryons, and the phenomenological status of a position-dependent deformation.
authors: Mahnaz Maleki, Asef Kheirandish, Morteza Nattagh Najafi, Hosein Mohammadzadeh

papers.title: Discrete truncated Wigner approximation of the quantum phase transition in the transverse-field Ising model
papers.abstract: The discrete truncated Wigner approximation (DTWA) has been a workhorse for large-scale spin dynamics, but whether it captures dynamics across a quantum phase transition has not been tested systematically. In this work, we use the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) to study the quantum phase transition with DTWA from one to three dimensions and with all-to-all connectivity, using slow linear ramps and fast ramps. We find that DTWA cannot capture the dynamics on the one-dimensional chain, and that its behavior is consistent with classical thermalization, in which its classical spins relax toward a thermal state at a finite effective temperature that does not vanish for slow ramps, while a one-dimensional chain cannot order at any finite temperature. For square and cubic lattices, in contrast to the chain, DTWA builds order, and the order sets in close to the quantum critical point found by quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, its correlations do not grow with the Kibble-Zurek exponents, so DTWA captures the onset of order but not the universal dynamics of the transition. For all-to-all coupling, DTWA follows the exact growth of the order parameter along the entire ramp. Our results suggest that DTWA becomes more reliable as each spin interacts with more partners, and that beyond one dimension it can indicate where a quantum phase transition lies but cannot capture its critical scaling.

papers.title: Quantum Advantage in Privacy-Preserving Hypothesis Testing via Entanglement-Assisted Classical Communication
papers.abstract: Quantum mechanisms satisfying quantum local differential privacy (QLDP) have been shown to achieve a quantum advantage over classical local differential privacy (LDP) mechanisms in certain hypothesis-testing problems. While previous demonstrations have considered the transmission of quantum states from users to a server, we investigate whether this advantage can persist under entanglement-assisted classical communication (EACC), where users and the server share entanglement in advance and communicate only classical messages. We formulate an EACC-based hypothesis-testing framework and introduce measurement local differential privacy (MLDP) to protect private inputs against arbitrary shared quantum states and server-side measurements. We establish that QLDP classical-to-quantum channels admit MLDP-compliant EACC simulations and that, in the high-privacy regime, certain optimal QLDP mechanisms can be realized with one-bit classical communication, albeit using high-dimensional entanglement. We then demonstrate that a strict quantum advantage persists even when the pre-shared entanglement is restricted to a single qubit pair and each user communicates only one classical bit. Using EACC protocols based on the geometry of qubit measurements, we establish this advantage for both asymmetric and symmetric hypothesis testing and every input alphabet of size $v \geq 3$ in the high-privacy limit. The ratio of the achieved error exponent to the optimal one under the LDP constraint is at least $5/4$ for all such alphabets and approaches $3/2$ as $v$ grows. These results demonstrate that quantum advantage in locally private hypothesis testing can persist under simultaneous constraints on entanglement dimension and classical communication.
authors: Ji-Ho Jung, Seung-Hyun Nam, Si-Hyeon Lee

papers.title: On the level lines of bilayer potentials with a finite number of harmonics
papers.abstract: We consider ``bilayer'' potentials formed by the superposition of two periodic potentials in a plane. We assume that both potentials share the same rotational symmetry and employ an approximation involving a finite number of harmonics in their Fourier expansions. An analysis of the level lines of the resulting quasiperiodic potential (a problem posed by S.P. Novikov) near the percolation threshold makes it possible to describe the behavior of large-scale closed level lines in this limit. The results presented here can also be applied to broader classes of bilayer potentials that possess ``good'' analytical properties.

papers.title: Minimal input dimension for superactivation of one-shot zero-error quantum capacity
papers.abstract: The one-shot zero-error quantum capacity $\overline{Q}_0$ is studied within the framework of noncommutative graphs of quantum channels. The additivity of $\overline{Q}_0$ is proved for an arbitrary finite collection of channels with two-dimensional input spaces. An explicit pair of noncommutative graphs $S,T\subset M_3$ exhibiting superactivation of the one-shot zero-error quantum capacity is also constructed. Together, these results establish that the minimum input dimension for such superactivation is $3$.

papers.title: Prethermalization of entanglement entropy in the mixed-field Ising model
papers.abstract: We study how weak integrability breaking affects the dynamics of the half-chain entanglement entropy of random product states in the mixed-field Ising model. The associated Hamiltonian depends on two parameters $g$ and $h$ determining the sizes of the longitudinal and transverse fields and has two integrable limits: the classical Ising chain $(h=0)$ and the transverse-field Ising model $(g=0)$. Weak perturbations of these limits give rise to the short-range network (SRN) and long-range network (LRN) regimes, respectively. We characterize the departure from integrable dynamics and the emergence of intermediate entanglement plateaus by melting times $T_M$ at prescribed entropy thresholds and analyze their dependence on the perturbation strength. For the SRN parameters examined away from $g=2$, we find $T_M\propto h^{-2}$ over the thresholds tested. At $g=2$, the relaxation splits into two stages: an initial departure from the integrable plateau with $T_M\propto h^{-1}$, followed by the melting of a well-defined intermediate prethermal plateau with $T_{M_2}\propto h^{-2}$. In the LRN regime, by contrast, the inverse of $T_M$ scales with exponents of $g$ close to either one or two, depending on the parameter values, the system size, and the entropy threshold, and no well-defined prethermal plateaus are observed. Our analysis distinguishes the melting of integrable dynamics from the subsequent decay of a prethermal plateau, which is observed in the SRN regime.
authors: Miguel Gonzalez, Budhaditya Bhattacharjee, Alexei Andreanov, Barbara Dietz, Sergej Flach

papers.title: A Path Integral Method with Far-Field Expansion for Open Quantum Dynamics
papers.abstract: We establish a connection between the quasi-adiabatic propagator path integral (QuAPI) method and fast resummation of Dyson series (FRODS). Building on this connection, we introduce a path integral method with far-field expansion (PIFFE) for quantum systems coupled linearly to a thermal Gaussian bath. PIFFE combines QuAPI with a Taylor expansion of the far-field bath influence, keeping interactions within $r$ time steps in exponential form. The scheme has error $O(\Delta t^2)$ at fixed final time and is free of stochastic or tensor-compression errors. Spin-boson tests show that PIFFE gives results much closer to QuAPI than FRODS does, even for small $r$, while requiring substantially less storage than QuAPI. This allows much longer bath memory lengths and simulations of multilevel systems. Truncating the bath memory and limiting the total auxiliary degree further reduce storage and computational costs.

papers.title: Defect Correlators from Supergravity: Finding the Missing Contact Terms
papers.abstract: We resolve a puzzle in the computation of holographic correlators using supergravity when defects are present. Previous direct supergravity calculations of defect two-point functions were found to differ from bootstrap results by a set of contact contributions. We show that the discrepancy arises from two effects: nonlinear Kaluza-Klein field redefinitions in the bulk, which induce additional quadratic couplings when applied consistently to localized sources, and off-shell terms in mixed bulk--defect vertices, which can collapse internal defect propagators. We demonstrate how these two mechanisms resolve the puzzle in two concrete examples in 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM, where we consider two-point correlators in the presence of a $\frac{1}{2}$-BPS Wilson line and on $\mathbb{RP}^4$.

papers.title: Higher derivatives and ghosts through three centuries
papers.abstract: We outline the history of the research of dynamic systems including higher derivatives in the Lagrangian, The story starts in 1744 when Euler published a book where the Euler--Lagrange differential equations for a HD system were first written. The next important landmarks were the papers of Ostrogradsky (1850) and of Pais and Uhlenbeck (1950). Many articles written in the second half of the last century were influenced by a misconception that was widespread at the time --- it was believed that higher derivatives necessarily bring about a violation of unitarity. We understand today that this is not the case and there are many systems with benign ghosts where HD are present but unitarity is not violated. In this review, we present and discuss several examples of such (quantum) mechanical systems and 2D field theories. Then we will briefly discuss higher-derivative gravity theories in 4 dimensions. In that case, the question whether the ghosts there are benign or not has a special status due to the absence of a nonperturbative Hamiltonian and does not have a definite answer yet. However, if one restricts oneself to classical theory, one can argue that the ghosts {\it are} benign (benign classical ghostly system is a system that needs an infinite time to reach a singularity, and it seems to the case both in ordinary and in HD gravity: the cosmic censorship conjecture implies that the singularities are always surrounded by horizons, and it takes an infinite time on the clocks of a distant observer to reach a horizon). Finally, I discuss supersymmetric HD theories: conformal supergravity, where the ghosts are also probably benign, and then an interesting supersymmetric HD gauge theory in 6 dimensions. It involves a dimensionless coupling constant, is renormalizable and rather beautiful. Unfortunately, it is not unitary --- ghosts are not benign there.

papers.title: Colored Jones polynomial of figure eight knot and non-perturbative topological recursion
papers.abstract: The asymptotic expansion of the colored Jones polynomial of the figure eight knot is proved to be connected with non-perturbative topological recursion on the underlying elliptic spectral curve, following the proposal of Borot and Eynard.

papers.title: Schwinger-Dyson recursion, Gr\"obner elimination and graph combinatorics
papers.abstract: Schwinger-Dyson equations are a cornerstone of quantum field theory (QFT). Derived using integration by parts, they capture relations between correlators of different orders, forming an open, infinite-dimensional system. In zero-dimensional QFTs with polynomial actions, which is just a physical interpretation for multivariate Gaussian integrals with polynomial insertions, conventional Gr\"obner elimination can be used to express all higher-order correlators (moments) in terms of a fixed basis set. One consequence is a closed finite-dimensional system of differential equations for the coupling dependence of these `master' correlators. An important application of zero-dimensional QFTs is in counting discrete geometric structures (as in simplicial approaches to quantum gravity). For the problem of counting labelled regular graphs, applying this Schwinger-Dyson closure results in a computational breakthrough relative to the existing state-of-the-art: for 9- and 10-regular graphs on $n$ vertices, a finite-depth, finite-width recursive formulation is obtained, making it possible to compute the total graph counts in $O(n)$ arithmetic operations.

papers.title: Reconstructing massive quivers on a defect circle
papers.abstract: We study the kink and particle spectra for the massive $\phi_{2,1}$-deformations of minimal models $\mathcal M_{k+1,k+2}$ via truncated conformal space approach (TCSA) on a defect circle. The massive $\phi_{2,1}$-deformation preserves a set of non-invertible symmetries, furnishing a fusion category $\mathcal C_k\simeq {\rm SO}(3)_k$. These non-invertible symmetries are spontaneously broken, and thus label the vacua and organize the kinks and particles into their multiplets in terms of quiver diagrams. We employ a finite-volume truncated Hamiltonian approach on defect Hilbert spaces, $\mathcal H_{X_i}$ for $X_i\in\mathcal C_k$, to study these quivers in the IR theories. The symmetry defect can then close an individual kink on a circle. We first establish the relation between states of definite fractional momentum on the defect circle and physical kink and particle states labelled by their vacuum pairs. Using form factors of local fields, we independently measure the squared amplitudes between the states of the two bases in defect TCSA. Combining these measurements with defect TCSA spectra, we reconstruct the quiver diagrams for $k=3,4,5$ without assuming them in advance. In particular, for $k=4$ we reconstruct the distinct quivers of the ordered and disordered phases. For $k=5$, we identify the quivers of both the light and heavy multiplets.

papers.title: Real-Time Cryo-CMOS Photon-Number Readout from a Single SNSPD
papers.abstract: Measurements leveraging the intrinsic photon-number resolution of Superconducting Nanostrip Single-Photon Detectors (SNSPDs) have recently gained traction due to the simplicity of the detector design. Intrinsic photon-number measurement schemes using SNSPDs encode the photon-number information in picosecond signal timing; these systems thus require high bandwidth readout and sensitive electrical measurement equipment. We show a cryogenic electronic circuit operating close to the SNSPD in the cryostat, which can isolate single-photon detection events directly from the SNSPD signal. This reduces the latency of the photon-number readout to (13.9 $\pm$ 0.3) ns, which enables feedforward operations based on intrinsic photon-number measurements with low latency.
authors: Niklas Lamberty, Dileep V. Reddy, Aishi Barua, Martin J. Stevens, Tim J. Bartley

papers.title: Coefficient-Range Mitigation on an 8-Bit Coherent Ising Machine
papers.abstract: Mapping optimization problems to the restricted coefficient range of an 8-bit CIM can distort their encoded energy landscapes. We investigate whether three coefficient-range mitigation techniques previously studied for quantum annealing---interaction extension, bounded-coefficient encoding, and augmented Lagrangian penalties---improve end-to-end optimization outcomes. Experiments on weighted Max-Cut, multidimensional knapsack, and quadratic assignment show that the benefits are selective. At a fixed number of CIM calls, intermediate interaction extension yields higher mean best Max-Cut objectives, whereas aggressive extension degrades performance. Bounded-coefficient encoding improves the mean best feasible profit on one knapsack instance but not the other. Augmented Lagrangian perturbations increase feasibility when unshifted constraint penalties are too weak, but do not outperform the best unshifted penalty setting. Overall, coefficient-range mitigation is most effective when its strength is tuned to the problem and encoding, with aggressive mitigation potentially offsetting its benefits.
authors: Manuel Radons, Lars Simon, Raoul Heese, Kensuke Inaba, Toshimori Honjo, Hiroki Takesue, Andreas Wilke

papers.title: Beyond-quantum correlations for single system in pseudo-quantum model
papers.abstract: Within the standard prepare-measure framework, it has been demonstrated that certain compositions of two elementary quantum systems can produce beyond-quantum correlations and can even lead to perfect discrimination of two non-orthogonal quantum states. In this Letter, we introduce the pseudo-quantum model (PQM) for a single system that incorporates the \emph{pseudo-states (effects)} (they satisfy all the properties of quantum states and effects except having negative eigenvalues), and yields valid probability. We consider a prepare-measure communication game known as random access code (RAC) and demonstrate that the success probability achievable within PQM exceeds the corresponding optimal quantum success probability, thereby giving rise to beyond-quantum correlations even for a single system. We then show that such correlations are unphysical as they violate the information causality (IC) principle. Moreover, we demonstrate that two non-orthogonal states can be perfectly distinguishable in PQM for a single system. Therefore, we demonstrate that for a single indivisible system (devoid of any composition), the negativity of \emph{pseudo-states (effects)} can lead to the emergence of beyond-quantum correlations.
authors: Vishnu Purushothaman, Akarshit Baranwal, Rohit Sarma Sarkar, A. K. Pan

papers.title: Lorentz charges for Lovelock gravity
papers.abstract: In this paper, we construct the charges associated with the residual local Lorentz transformations on a black hole horizon in the Lovelock class of theories of gravity. The horizons is assumed to be non- expanding horizons, \emph{i.e} a null hypersurface for which the expansion corresponding to the null generator vanish. Naturally, these hypersurfaces preserve only a subgroup of the full Lorentz group of the bulk, and the residual symmetries correspond to the little group which stabilizes the horizon null generator. We show that on the horizon, the Hamiltonian charge corresponding to the residual local Lorentz boost is the Wald entropy.
authors: Ayan Chatterjee, Sahil Devdutt, Amit Ghosh, Avirup Ghosh

papers.title: Simultaneous Inversion of Drift and Potential in the Fractional Magnetic Schr\"odinger Equation
papers.abstract: We study the Calder\'on problem for the fractional magnetic Schr\"odinger equation with drift in the bivariate additive framework. When the magnetic potential $A$ is known and fixed, we prove that the drift $b$ and the scalar potential $q$ can be simultaneously and uniquely determined from exterior Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements. When $A$ is unknown, we prove that the triple $(A,b,q)$ can only be recovered up to a natural gauge equivalence class, and that the drift $b$ is a gauge invariant, hence uniquely determined. The proofs rely on the Alessandrini identity, Runge approximation, and the unique continuation property for fractional magnetic operators. Furthermore, we have developed a numerical reconstruction framework that combines finite difference discretization, radial basis function surrogate modeling, and smoothed TV regularization. One-dimensional and two-dimensional numerical examples have verified the effectiveness of the proposed method and supported the theoretical uniqueness result.
authors: Yun-Long Liu, Jin Wen, Jun-Liang Fu, Xue-Juan Ren

papers.title: Generic non-convergence of low-temperature Ising Glauber dynamics on $\mathbb Z^2$
papers.abstract: We study how typical convergence is, in the topological sense of Baire category, for the heat-bath Glauber dynamics of the nearest-neighbour, zero-field Ising model on $\mathbb Z^2$ started from translation-invariant initial laws. At sufficiently low positive temperature, we show that the initial laws whose evolution has both the plus and the minus phase as weak subsequential limits form a dense $G_\delta$ subset of the space of translation-invariant laws with the weak topology. Consequently, the initial laws for which the dynamics converges in distribution form a meagre set, which gives a partial answer to an open problem posed by Liggett. In particular, a large initial magnetisation does not force convergence to the plus phase, even for spatially ergodic initial laws. The proof combines equilibrium and mixing estimates of Gheissari and Sly with a periodic grid of plus spins of vanishing density and Baire's theorem, and it applies to all reversible monotone Glauber dynamics for the Ising model.

papers.title: Scaling laws for quantum reflection of hydrogen isotopes on silicon
papers.abstract: Quantum reflection is a counter-intuitive process occurring when an atom is reflected by a rapidly-varying attraction towards a surface, for example the Casimir-Polder force. The reflection probability depends on the attractive potential and on the mass of the atom. For hydrogen isotopes, the potentials are nearly identical whereas significant differences in quantum reflection come from the effect of atomic mass. We calculate the quantum reflection probability for the three isotopes H, D or T falling onto the plane surface of an intrinsic silicon bulk. We show that the results obey scaling laws determined by scattering lengths calculated from theory. Moreover the scattering lengths also obey scaling laws with respect to atomic masses of the isotopes.

papers.title: Geometry, masking and selection in Differential Evolution and SOMA on quantum state manifolds
papers.abstract: Differential Evolution (DE) and the Self-Organizing Migrating Algorithm (SOMA) generate new candidates through vector arithmetic: they subtract population members, scale the difference, and mask coordinates. Many practical search spaces are not vector spaces, however. Rotation angles are periodic, normalized states lie on spheres and projective spaces, and circuit parameters are coupled through the quantum states they produce. We present a systematic study of how such geometry affects the core operations of DE and SOMA. Keeping the operators and selection rules fixed, we replace only their geometric primitives and separate the effects of difference construction, masking, and selection in a large paired numerical study covering textbook manifolds and variational quantum problems. Geometry-consistent differences make full-crossover (CR = 1) DE significantly better on 16 of 31 non-Euclidean configurations, with no significant deterioration, and the advantage persists when the measured computational cost of each variant is taken into account. The effect is largest where ordinary subtraction misrepresents distances between candidates: success on periodic synchronization rises from 44% to 100%, and on a positive-definite matrix problem from 1% to 99%. On six- qubit variational eigensolvers, shortest-path angular differences reduce the mean final loss by 90% for about 3% extra runtime. The improvements come with two contrasting diversity patterns, more effective population contraction or preserved population diversity, so higher acceptance rates do not necessarily indicate better search. Crossover masks interact with geometry: they can favor cheaper retractions and can increase the distance moved in quantum-state space when circuit parameters are coupled. These results give practical rules for designing population-based optimizers on non-Euclidean and quantum search spaces.

papers.title: Ancilla-Assisted Accelerated Readout of Transmon Qubits
papers.abstract: We present a scheme for accelerating dispersive readout of superconducting transmon qubits. Dispersive readout works by weakly coupling the target transmon to a resonator, such that the resonator experiences a state-dependent frequency shift, which can then be read out. Our scheme introduces an ancillary transmon coupled to the same resonator. By appropriately correlating its state with that of the target transmon (using a fast CNOT gate), we show that the resonator frequency shift is approximately doubled, halving the required measurement duration to maintain the same quality. We present analytical results within the dispersive approximation, before employing and extending the recently introduced technique of branch analysis to account for ionization and other nonlinearities. Using this, and taking into account realistic noise and gate times, we show that our scheme allows measurement durations smaller by a factor of approximately 0.6, demonstrating that it offers a viable route for accelerating measurements of transmon qubits.
authors: Christopher Corlett, Noah Linden, Paul Skrzypczyk

papers.title: Patterns and correlations in time-reversal symmetry breaking
papers.abstract: Time-reversal symmetry (TRS) breaking is the hallmark of non-equilibrium statistical physics. This notwithstanding, in translationally invariant systems, it is almost always treated only as a global quantity. We propose to use the local entropy production rate as a spatio-temporal field to describe extended homogeneous non-equilibrium systems. We find that this field generically displays spatial correlations, with a typical length that grows as we approach some non-equilibrium phase transitions. We also show that the correlation length associated with the local entropy production rate follows heretofore unknown scaling laws involving control parameters as well as the observation time used for trajectories. Our work paves the way to the use of the local entropy production as a powerful observable to identify the scale and source of TRS breaking in non-equilibrium systems.
authors: Ido Patish, Mathias Casiulis, Dov Levine

papers.title: Fundamental Symmetries in Krein Spaces
papers.abstract: We study the space of fundamental symmetries of a real or complex Krein space in finite or infinite dimension. After recalling the equivalence of the associated Hilbert norms, we describe two global operator parametrizations and their relation. The space is realized as a Banach symmetric space under $m(J,J')=JJ'J$. Its canonical connection is the tangential projection of the flat derivative in the real Banach space of Krein-self-adjoint operators. This yields explicit formulas for geodesics, parallel transport, transvections, and curvature. The positive square roots $(JJ')^{1/2}$ implement both isometries between the associated Hilbert spaces and geodesic transvections. A proof of their intertwining property in an earlier publication is corrected.

papers.title: Quantum Algorithm for Direct Estimation of Energy-Level Differences via Quantum Dynamics Simulation
papers.abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for the early fault-tolerant quantum computing (early-FTQC) era that estimates minute energy-level differences, such as energy gradients and molecular forces, at a lower sampling cost than existing phase-estimation methods. Such energy derivatives, accessed as the small energy difference induced by an infinitesimal parameter shift, are central to quantum simulation in chemistry and materials science. Although Statistical Phase Estimation (SPE) is well-suited to energy estimation in this era, applying it to an energy difference demands a sampling complexity that scales with the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian, which grows with system size. Our algorithm overcomes this by incorporating two time-evolution operators, corresponding to the Hamiltonians before and after the parameter shift, into a single quantum circuit, which is combined with a non-adaptive, statistically sampled reconstruction in the energy-difference domain. This reduces the relevant scale from the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian to that of the operator norm of the Hamiltonian derivative and the parameter shift, thereby lowering the sampling complexity. We further propose the joint estimation of energy eigenvalues and their differences, giving a holistic view of the energy landscape. Numerical simulations and resource estimations on prototypical systems, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, demonstrate the resulting reductions in required resources without compromising precision. This positions energy-difference estimation as a practical task for early-FTQC devices, opening a route to molecular forces, response properties, and excited-state energy differences.
authors: Norifumi Matsumoto, Yuya O. Nakagawa, Shota Kanasugi, Yuichiro Hidaka, Kazunori Maruyama, Hirotaka Oshima

papers.title: Magnetization, susceptibility, and entanglement entropy in antiferromagnetic star-shaped homometallic tetranuclear and pentanuclear Cu(II) complexes
papers.abstract: We present a theoretical investigation of the magnetization, magnetic susceptibility, and quantum entanglement entropy in antiferromagnetic star-shaped tetranuclear ($Cu_4$) and pentanuclear ($Cu_5$) Cu(II) clusters, motivated by experimentally realized molecular spin systems. In both cases, the study presents a discussion of the comparison between experimental data and theoretical analytical calculations of magnetic susceptibility as a function of temperature. The correlation between magnetization jumps and magnetic susceptibility peaks, along with the presence of entanglement entropy plateaus as a function of external magnetic fields, is analyzed in the low-temperature regime. Overall, the results demonstrate that the cluster size, geometry, and interaction anisotropy play a crucial role in shaping both the thermodynamic and the entanglement properties. In addition, the study is based on antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin Hamiltonians, with the inclusion of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.
authors: Gor Mirzoyan, Vladimir V. Papoyan, Andrea Trombettoni, Nikita Titov, Lev Ananikyan, Nerses Ananikian

papers.title: Sharp decay and regularity thresholds for Minkowski stability in spherical symmetry
papers.abstract: We establish sharp decay and regularity thresholds for Minkowski stability in the spherically symmetric Einstein--scalar field system. For small smooth characteristic data measured in weighted derivative seminorms, we prove global stability at borderline decay and half-derivative regularity of the initial data. The resulting developments remain uniformly close to Minkowski spacetime and are future causally geodesically complete. Both thresholds are sharp: below either the decay or regularity threshold, we construct arbitrarily small smooth, initially untrapped data whose developments contain trapped spheres.

papers.title: Search-for-Gradient: Search-Based Restarts for Optimisation in Structured Flat Landscapes of Variational Quantum Algorithms
papers.abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a promising class of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms that involve parameterised quantum circuits and classical optimisation. VQAs have found applications in simulation, optimisation, and machine learning. However, their scalability is hindered by flat landscapes-regions in the parameter space where gradients vanish exponentially small. In such regimes, gradient-based optimisation methods fail because parameter updates become ineffective in the absence of informative gradients. In this work, we propose a search-based restart framework to escape flat regions in structured flat landscapes, in which small trainable regions exist within a large flat landscape. This framework approaches the plateau escape as a search problem and locates trainable regions. The optimiser's parameters stop updating when the gradients vanish, and the method then searches over-sampled points to identify landscapes with nonzero gradients. We provide theoretical estimates of the number of jumps and the probability of escape from flat landscapes. This restarts the local optimisation process and avoids stagnation. We tested this framework on synthetic functions that mimic structured flat landscapes and a real quantum circuit cost landscape. Theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that Search-for-Gradient improves optimisation performance in structured flat landscapes. The proposed framework assumes the existence of a trainable region with nonzero measure and will not work if it has zero measure. Our framework can be integrated with existing VQAs to improve trainability and robustness.
authors: Subham Das, Bikash K. Behera, Andr\'es Camilo Granda Arango, Giuseppe Sergioli, Roberto Giuntini

papers.title: The transverse spin-gradient approximation in noncollinear spin density functional theory
papers.abstract:
We prove a quantitative error bound for a fixed-axis variant of the transverse spin-gradient approximation (TSGA) in noncollinear spin density functional theory. Inspired by Eich and Gross, we use a spin-spiral wave (SSW) as the local reference for the grand-canonical Levy-Lieb energy with the Hartree term subtracted. We construct the thermodynamic limit of the electron gas with constant total density and a prescribed SSW magnetization. Its energy per unit volume $e_{m SSW}$ is evaluated at the local wavevector $
abla\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the spiral phase. When $\varphi$ is the azimuthal angle of the magnetization $\mathbf{m}=(m_1,m_2,m_3)$, the approximation reads \[ E(ho,\mathbf{m})\approx\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}e_{m SSW} ig(ho(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{x}),
abla\varphi(\mathbf{x}) ig)\,d \mathbf{x}. \] Here $
abla\varphi$ measures the local rotation of $\mathbf{m}$ about the third axis. Wherever $m_1^2+m_2^2>0$, it equals $(m_1
abla m_2-m_2
abla m_1)/(m_1^2+m_2^2)$. The approximation thus depends only on the total density $ho$, the magnetization and its first derivatives. When the spin-polarized density in the rotating frame and the local wavevector vary on the length scale $N^{1/3}$, with $N$ the mean number of particles, we obtain an error $O(N^{5/6})$ for an energy of order $N$. Setting the phase to zero gives the noncollinear local spin density approximation (LSDA) for arbitrary magnetization directions.

papers.title: Cross-chip transfer in quantum photonic neural networks
papers.abstract: Fabrication variability makes it difficult to reuse one set of trained parameters across a batch of quantum photonic chips without additional chip-specific optimization. We examine how device-specific compensation and task tolerance shape cross-chip performance. For squared operator loss, local analysis predicts that reducing own-chip error through compensation incurs an increase in expected loss on independent chips. We use Monte Carlo ensemble training (MC-ENS), informed by an available statistical model of fabrication-induced parameter errors. It optimizes one shared parameter set for each task or target at a given fabrication scale by averaging losses over simulated chip realizations resampled from this model. Numerical simulations of a quantum photonic neural network compare MC-ENS with single-chip training, sharpness-aware training and a covariance-informed variant. For CNOT synthesis and Ising dynamics, MC-ENS reduces mean conditional process infidelity and increases mean postselection probability on unseen chips. In classification, high accuracy can persist despite substantial changes in the optical transformation. The decision-margin analysis shows when fabrication-induced score shifts are likely to change predicted labels. The trained shared parameters can be reused without device-specific retraining on unseen chips drawn from the same fabrication distribution.
authors: Iqra Bashir, Bikash K. Behera, Qi Qin, Keren Li

papers.title: On the performance of nanoscale detection methods in NV-center spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) in subfemtoliter volumes operates in a regime where statistical fluctuations of the nuclear magnetization can exceed its thermal mean. Solid-state quantum sensors such as nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are sensitive enough to detect NMR signals from such small volumes, which has motivated several detection protocols, based either on correlating the statistical polarization or on coherently detecting hyperpolarized samples. Here we bring Qdyne, CS, MCS, and CASR into a single framework for nanoscale samples. Specifically, we derive a unified analytical expression for the SNR and spin-number sensitivity applicable to all four protocols under consistent experimental conditions. Numerical simulations of the full measurement sequences confirm this expression over the whole range of parameters explored. This formulation enables a quantitative comparison of their performance while accounting for the distinct measurement sequences, acquisition times, and other related parameters. Using the SNR and the spin-number sensitivity as figures of merit, we identify which protocol performs best in each experimental regime, thereby providing a practical guide for choosing and tuning the most suitable method for a given experiment.
authors: Koushik Paul, Pol Alsina-Bol\'ivar, Jorge Casanova

papers.title: Squeezing-preserving coherent control in Fourier-shaped optical lattices
papers.abstract: Motional squeezed states of atoms in optical lattices are affected by the anharmonicity of the trapping potential. Unequal vibrational energy spacings cause dephasing among the occupied motional-state coherences, leading to distortion of the wavepacket and a reduction in squeezing. We show numerically that adding a weak second or third spatial harmonic to a one-dimensional lattice slows the initial decay of the squeezing. Squeezed states are prepared by one or two sudden changes of the lattice depth. For each harmonic and each preparation scheme, we choose the harmonic amplitude that keeps the evolved state closest, on average over 1 ms, to its evolution in a harmonic trap. We then compare the squeezing with that in a sinusoidal lattice with the same initial squeezing and trap frequency. In all four cases studied, the successive squeezing maxima initially decay more slowly in the shaped lattice. The improvement arises because the optimal harmonic nearly equalizes the two dominant vibrational level spacings over the region occupied by the squeezed wave packet, which canceling the quartic term of the potential alone does not achieve. Because the amplitude of the added harmonic is static and can be produced with existing Fourier-synthesis techniques, lattice shaping offers a simple way to preserve motional squeezing without additional time-dependent control.
authors: Ko-Wei Cheng, Wui Seng Leong, Shau-Yu Lan

papers.title: Intrinsically nonlinear nanomechanical resonator toward the single-phonon Kerr regime
papers.abstract: Manipulating a physical system at the single-quantum level typically requires an anharmonic energy spectrum. Nanomechanical resonators, however, are commonly admitted to be linear objects in the single-phonon regime, thus motivating most efforts to employ external sources of nonlinearity at the cost of added relaxation and decoherence channels. Here, we take a radically different approach by directly exploiting strong intrinsic mechanical nonlinearities. We quantify this nonlinearity using a novel method based on the coupling between bending modes. Using this technique, we establish an upper bound of 34.0 +/- 9.7 phonons for the onset of intrinsically mechanical bistability. In addition, we highlight a new tuning mechanism based on a mechanical polarization angle of an upward-buckled nanotube resonator allowing us to reach an optimal working point. Extrapolating this level of intrinsic nonlinearity to realistically shorter resonators shows that the single-phonon Kerr regime is within reach, allowing for the realization of purely mechanical Schr\"odinger-cat states and highly coherent mechanical qubits.
authors: S. Klingel, T. Althuon, C. Wassmer, C. S\"urgers, T. Cubaynes, W. Wernsdorfer

papers.title: Unfreezing topology using out-of-equilibrium replica exchanges
